unit.unitOverview: You are the host, and then you are the guest. Offer a thing and invite someone: Would you like a mug of tea? Give a short set of instructions, and say what not to do. Check that you are right: The kettle is ready, isn't it?
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen and repeat.
Words: listen, look and say. 30 words.
Patterns: 3 cards. Read the one done for you.
Reading: a visit, a kitchen page and a notice.
Speaking: tap the mic. Say it. Listen.
Writing: an invitation, six steps, a notice and two replies.
Practice: 6 exercises. Check with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. At the end, My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 2: Offers, Instructions and Checking.
In this unit you are the host, and then you are the guest.
A host invites people and looks after them. A guest visits.
There are three new things to say. Here they are.
One: the short question on the end.
You know this sentence: You work here.
Now add two words: You work here, don't you?
Those two words are a tag.
A tag checks that you are right.
The sentence is positive, so the tag is negative.
You work here, don't you?
The tray is clean, isn't it?
They are ready, aren't they?
She has a mug, doesn't she?
Now the other way.
The sentence is negative, so the tag is positive.
It isn't far, is it?
You don't drive, do you?
He can't come, can he?
One side is positive and the other side is negative.
Never both the same.
A comma goes before the tag. A question mark goes at the end.
Two: would you like.
Use would you like and a thing, to offer that thing.
Would you like a biscuit?
Would you like a mug of tea?
Would you like some water from the jug?
Now use would you like, then to and a doing word, to invite.
Would you like to sit here?
Would you like to come on Friday?
Would you like to see the office?
The answers are short.
Yes please. Or: No thank you.
Both answers are kind. You can always say no thank you.
Three: instructions, two kinds.
You know the first kind: Press the switch.
The doing word comes first, and there is no you.
Now the other kind: Don't press it yet.
Put don't in front of the doing word.
Give two or three steps in order.
First, fill the kettle.
Then press the switch.
Don't open it. It is very hot.
Finally, pour the water into the mug.
Now the words. There are thirty.
Some are for the host: offer, invite, guest, host, accept, refuse, welcome, serve.
Some are small things to offer: a biscuit, a napkin, a tray, a sandwich, a snack, a jug, a mug, a kettle.
Some are careful instructions: press, pull, push, twist, slide, switch, careful, ready.
And six are for checking: certain, correct, wrong, meaning, confirm, clear.
Last, one word about checking.
If you are not certain, say so. That is not a mistake.
Ask: What is the meaning of this word?
Or ask: Do you mean the small one?
Or use a tag: You said Friday, didn't you?
Then you know you are correct, and nothing goes wrong.
Now go to the Words page.
Listen, and say each word after the voice.

readings.title: A Guest at the Door
readings.setting: Lena works from home. Her colleague Omar comes for a box of papers.
readings.passageScript:
Omar came at ten. Lena opened the door.
Lena: Welcome, Omar. Come in.
Omar: Thank you. It is cold outside, isn't it?
Lena: It is. Would you like a mug of tea?
Omar: Yes please. A small one.
Lena filled the kettle and pressed the switch.
Lena: Sit near the window. That chair is the warm one.
Omar: Thank you. You work from home every day, don't you?
Lena: Most days. On Tuesday I go to the office.
The kettle was ready. Lena put two mugs on a tray.
She added a jug of milk, some biscuits and two napkins.
Lena: Would you like a biscuit?
Omar: No thank you. I had a snack on the bus.
They talked for twenty minutes. Then Omar looked at his watch.
Omar: I must go. The box is by the door, isn't it?
Lena: It is. Be careful. It is heavy.
Omar: Thank you for the tea.
Lena: You are welcome. Come again on Friday.

readings.title: How to Make Tea for a Guest
readings.setting: A page on the wall of a small office kitchen.
readings.passageScript:
HOW TO MAKE TEA FOR A GUEST
Read all six steps first. Then start.
1. Fill the kettle with cold water. Don't fill it to the top.
2. Press the switch at the back. Don't press it two times.
3. Wait. The kettle takes about two minutes.
4. Don't open the kettle. It is very hot.
5. Put one tea bag in each mug. Pour the water slowly.
6. Wait two minutes. Then take the tea bag out.
Milk is in the fridge. The jug is on the second shelf.
Biscuits are in the blue box, next to the tray.
Before you carry the tray, check three things.
Are the mugs clean? Is the jug full? Are there napkins?
Careful: the mugs are hot. Carry the tray slowly, with two hands.
When you are ready, take the tray to your guest.
Wash everything after, and put it back.

grammar.title: Checking with a tag on the end: it is warm, isn't it?
grammar.explanation:
A tag is two short words at the end of a sentence.
It turns your sentence into a small question.
You use it to check that you are right.
If the sentence is positive, the tag is negative.
If the sentence is negative, the tag is positive.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Positive sentence, negative tag:
You work here, don't you?
It is warm, isn't it?
They are ready, aren't they?
She has a mug, doesn't she?
You went home, didn't you?
I can wait, can't I?

Negative sentence, positive tag:
It isn't far, is it?
You don't drive, do you?
He can't come, can he?
They weren't ready, were they?

A comma goes before the tag.
A question mark goes at the end.
grammar.workedExample:
Make a tag for: The kettle is hot.
1. Find the verb: is.
2. The sentence is positive, so the tag is negative: isn't.
3. Say the thing in one short word: the kettle becomes it.
4. Put the tag after a comma: The kettle is hot, isn't it?

Now a negative one: The tray isn't clean.
1. The verb is isn't, so the tag is positive: is.
2. The thing is the tray: it.
3. The tray isn't clean, is it?
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to say the whole sentence again.
No: The tray is clean, is the tray clean?
Yes: The tray is clean, isn't it?
Two words only: the verb and one short word for the thing.
grammar.memoryTip: One side positive, the other side negative. Never both the same.
grammar.practice:
Write the two words of the tag.
1. You work here, ___ ___?
2. The kettle is hot, ___ ___?
3. It isn't far, ___ ___?
4. They are ready, ___ ___?
5. She doesn't drive, ___ ___?
6. You went home late, ___ ___?
7. He can't come, ___ ___?
8. The mugs were clean, ___ ___?
grammar.answerKey:
1. don't you  2. isn't it  3. is it  4. aren't they  5. does she  6. didn't you  7. can he  8. weren't they
Wrong on 3, 5 or 7? Those sentences are already negative, so the tag has no not.
Wrong on 6? There is no do word in You went home late, so the tag uses did.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read this card again, then do it once more.

grammar.title: Offering and inviting: would you like a mug?
grammar.explanation:
Would you like is a kind way to offer and to invite.
Put a thing after it to offer that thing.
Put to and a doing word after it to invite someone.
The answers are short: yes please, or no thank you.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Offer a thing: would you like, then the thing.
Would you like a biscuit?
Would you like a mug of tea?
Would you like some water?

Invite: would you like, then to and a doing word.
Would you like to sit here?
Would you like to come on Friday?
Would you like to see the garden?

The answers:
Yes please. Yes please, a small one.
No thank you. No thank you, I have one.

Would you like never changes.
Not: would you likes. Not: do you would like.
grammar.workedExample:
You have a tray of biscuits. Offer one.
1. Start: Would you like.
2. Add the thing: Would you like a biscuit?
3. The guest answers: Yes please.

Now invite the same guest to sit down.
1. Start: Would you like.
2. Add to and the doing word: Would you like to sit down?
3. The guest answers: No thank you, I will stand.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to leave out to in an invitation.
No: Would you like sit here?
Yes: Would you like to sit here?
A thing needs no to. A doing word always needs to.
grammar.memoryTip: A thing straight after like. A doing word after to.
grammar.practice:

2. Would you like ___? (sit near the window)
3. Would you like ___? (a napkin)

5. Would you like ___? (some water from the jug)
6. Would you like ___? (see the new office)
Now write the answer. Use yes please or no thank you.
7. Would you like a biscuit? (yes)
8. Would you like to wait here? (no)
grammar.answerKey:
1. a mug of tea  2. to sit near the window  3. a napkin  4. to come on Saturday  5. some water from the jug  6. to see the new office  7. Yes please.  8. No thank you.
Wrong on 2, 4 or 6? Those are doing words, so they need to in front.
Wrong on 7 or 8? The answer is two or three words, not a whole sentence.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read this card again, then do it once more.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: Press it, then don't pull it: steps in order
grammar.explanation:
An instruction starts with the doing word: Press the switch.
To say what not to do, put don't in front of it.
Don't press that yet.
Give your steps in order, one on each line.
Say the careful step before the step it is about.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Positive: the doing word comes first.
Fill the kettle.
Press the switch.
Slide the tray to the left.

Negative: don't, then the doing word.
Don't press that yet.
Don't pull the door. Push it.
Don't open it. It is hot.

In order:
First, fill the kettle.
Then press the switch.
Don't open it yet.
Finally, pour the water into the mug.

Do not is the long form. Don't is the short form.
After don't, the doing word never changes.
grammar.workedExample:
Show a guest how to open your door.
1. Step one, a doing word: Put the key in.
2. Step two: Turn the key to the left.
3. Say what to avoid: Don't pull the door.
4. Step three: Push it slowly.
5. Now put them in order with then and finally.

Put the key in. Then turn it to the left.
Don't pull the door. Finally, push it slowly.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to add you, or an -s, to an instruction.
No: You press the switch. No: Presses the switch.
Yes: Press the switch.
And no is not used here: No press it. Say: Don't press it.
grammar.memoryTip: Doing word first. For the other kind, don't comes first.
grammar.practice:

B. Don't open it. It is very hot.
C. First, fill the kettle with cold water.
D. Finally, pour the water into the mug.

Now write the negative form of each instruction.
6. Press that switch.
7. Pull the door.
8. Put the jug on the tray.
grammar.answerKey:
Order: C, A, E, B, D.
6. Don't press that switch.  7. Don't pull the door.  8. Don't put the jug on the tray.
First, then and finally tell you the order. The hot step comes before you pour.
After don't, the doing word never changes: don't presses is wrong.
All right: good. Three or fewer: read this card again and do it once more.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Choose the tag
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose the correct tag.
1. You work here, (don't you / do you)?
2. It isn't far, (isn't it / is it)?
3. They are ready, (are they / aren't they)?
4. She doesn't drive, (does she / doesn't she)?
5. The tea is hot, (is it / isn't it)?
6. He can't come, (can he / can't he)?
7. You went home late, (didn't you / don't you)?
8. The mugs weren't clean, (were they / weren't they)?
activities.answerSummary:
1. don't you  2. is it  3. aren't they  4. does she  5. isn't it  6. can he  7. didn't you  8. were they
One side is positive and the other side is negative. Never both the same.
Wrong on 7? The sentence uses went, a past form, so the tag uses did.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read Pattern 1 again and do this once more.

activities.title: Practice 2 — A thing, or to and a doing word
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write to where it is needed. Write nothing where it is not.

2. Would you like ___ sit near the window?
3. Would you like ___ some water?
4. Would you like ___ come on Friday?
5. Would you like ___ a clean napkin?
6. Would you like ___ see the garden?
7. Would you like ___ a mug of tea?
8. Would you like ___ wait inside?
activities.answerSummary:
to: 2, 4, 6 and 8.  Nothing: 1, 3, 5 and 7.
A thing after would you like needs no to: a biscuit, some water.
A doing word always needs to: to sit, to come, to see, to wait.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read Pattern 2 again and do this once more.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Do it, or don't do it
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the instruction. Use the word in brackets.
1. (press) ___ the switch at the back.
2. (not pull) ___ the door. Push it.
3. (slide) ___ the tray to the middle.
4. (not open) ___ the kettle. It is hot.

6. (not put) ___ the hot jug on the paper.

1. Press  2. Don't pull  3. Slide  4. Don't open  5. Twist  6. Don't put  7. Push  8. Don't press
After Don't, the doing word never changes: Don't pulls is wrong.
An instruction has no you at the start and no -s at the end.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read Pattern 3 again and do this once more.

activities.answerSummary:
1. Wrong: Would you like to sit down?
2. Correct.
3. Wrong: Don't press that switch.
4. Correct.
5. Correct.
6. Wrong: They are ready, aren't they?
7. Correct.
8. Correct.

2. What do you say at the desk?

quizzes.question: Which sentence has the correct tag?
quizzes.options: You work here, don't you? | You work here, do you? | You work here, don't he? | You work here, isn't it?
quizzes.explanation: The sentence is positive, so the tag is negative: don't. The short word for you is you, not he or it. Do you leaves both sides positive.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: It isn't far, ___?
quizzes.options: isn't it | is it | it is | does it
quizzes.explanation: The sentence is negative, so the tag is positive: is it. Isn't it would make both sides negative. It is is a statement, not a tag. Does it needs a do sentence, and this one uses is.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: Which sentence is correct?
quizzes.options: She doesn't drive, doesn't she? | She doesn't drive, she does? | She doesn't drive, does she? | She drive, does she?
quizzes.explanation: A negative sentence takes a positive tag: does she. Doesn't she keeps both sides negative. She does? is not a tag. She drive has no -s and no doesn't.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: You want to offer a biscuit. What do you say?
quizzes.options: Would you like to a biscuit? | Would you like biscuit? | You would like a biscuit. | Would you like a biscuit?
quizzes.explanation: A thing after would you like needs no to. Biscuit needs a in front of it. You would like is a sentence about the guest, not an offer.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: You want to invite someone to sit down. What do you say?
quizzes.options: Would you like to sit here? | Would you like sit here? | Would you like a sit here? | You like to sit here?
quizzes.correctAnswer: Would you like to sit here?
quizzes.explanation: A doing word after would you like always needs to. Sit is a doing word, so a sit is wrong. You like to sit here is a question about every day, not an invitation.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: Someone offers you tea and you do not want it. What do you say?
quizzes.options: No, I refuse. | No thank you. | No, thanks you. | Not please.
quizzes.explanation: No thank you is the short, kind answer. Refuse is a word for talking about it, not for saying it. Thanks you and Not please are not English.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: Which line tells someone NOT to do something?
quizzes.options: Press the switch. | Please press the switch. | Don't press the switch. | You press the switch.
quizzes.explanation: Don't in front of the doing word says what not to do. The other three all say to do it. You press also adds a you, which an instruction does not need.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: ___ that switch yet. It is not ready.
quizzes.options: Not press | No press | Don't presses | Don't press
quizzes.explanation: Don't comes first, and the doing word does not change. Not press and No press are not English. Presses adds an -s that an instruction never has.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: Fill the kettle. Press the switch. Don't open it. Pour the water. Which step says what not to do?
quizzes.options: Don't open it. | Fill the kettle. | Press the switch. | Pour the water.
quizzes.explanation: Only one step starts with don't, and that is the step to avoid. The other three all say to do something.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: A guest arrives at your door. What do you say first?
quizzes.options: Goodbye. See you soon. | Welcome. Come in. | No thank you. | It is ready, isn't it?
quizzes.explanation: A host welcomes the guest at the door. Goodbye ends a visit. No thank you answers an offer. A tag question checks a fact, and nothing has been said yet.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: What does confirm mean?
quizzes.options: To say no to a thing. | To bring food to a table. | To say again that something is correct. | To make a mistake.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To say again that something is correct.
quizzes.explanation: Confirm means you check a fact and say it is correct. Saying no is refuse. Bringing food to a table is serve. Making a mistake is being wrong.

quizzes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
quizzes.question: A notice says: PULL. Don't push. The door does not open. What do you do?
quizzes.options: Push the door harder. | Press the door. | Twist the door. | Pull the door.
quizzes.explanation: The notice says PULL and Don't push, so pull it. Pressing and twisting are different moves. The notice does not ask for either of them.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. Speaking 5 is the listening check: it is meant to be played once and acted on before the written steps are read. If you are helping, listen to the recordings together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.noteType: The two errors worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: First, the tag that agrees with its sentence: They are ready, are they? Both halves end up positive, and the learner cannot usually hear it. Pattern 1's tip line is the whole rule, and Practice 1 sets the two tags side by side so the choice has to be made rather than guessed. Second, the missing to in an invitation: Would you like sit here? Pattern 2 splits offering from inviting for exactly this reason, and Practice 2 is the drill. Say the line aloud both ways; the wrong one is easier to hear than to see.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: The people, the office, the building and the notice are all made up, and Writing 1, 3 and 4 say plainly that the name, the day and the place can be invented. No task asks for a real address, a real workplace or a real name. Speaking 3 offers at work, at school or at home, so a learner with no job is never stuck for a task.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Tags are taught with is, are, was, were, do, does, did and can only. Tags on will, shall and have are not taught here and are not asked for anywhere in the practice. Would you like is taught as a whole phrase for offering and inviting; would for polite requests comes later. The sequence words first, then and finally are known from Level 1 Unit 15 and are used here without a card, and so is the plain positive instruction; what is new in Pattern 3 is the negative one and the two kinds in one short set.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.noteType: Hot water and the AI tutor
teacherNotes.note: The kettle appears in the reading, the writing model and several practice items because it is the clearest small machine an adult already knows. Every hot step in this unit carries a careful line or a Don't line, and that wording is worth keeping if the learner rewrites the steps. The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task here is scored by it alone. Never ask it to confirm a real address, a real workplace or a real name.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: You work here, don't you? — The sentence is positive, so the tag is negative: don't. The short word for you is you, not he or it. Do you leaves both sides positive.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: is it — The sentence is negative, so the tag is positive: is it. Isn't it would make both sides negative. It is is a statement, not a tag. Does it needs a do sentence, and this one uses is.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She doesn't drive, does she? — A negative sentence takes a positive tag: does she. Doesn't she keeps both sides negative. She does? is not a tag. She drive has no -s and no doesn't.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Would you like a biscuit? — A thing after would you like needs no to. Biscuit needs a in front of it. You would like is a sentence about the guest, not an offer.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Would you like to sit here? — A doing word after would you like always needs to. Sit is a doing word, so a sit is wrong. You like to sit here is a question about every day, not an invitation.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: No thank you. — No thank you is the short, kind answer. Refuse is a word for talking about it, not for saying it. Thanks you and Not please are not English.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Don't press the switch. — Don't in front of the doing word says what not to do. The other three all say to do it. You press also adds a you, which an instruction does not need.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Don't press — Don't comes first, and the doing word does not change. Not press and No press are not English. Presses adds an -s that an instruction never has.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Don't open it. — Only one step starts with don't, and that is the step to avoid. The other three all say to do something.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Welcome. Come in. — A host welcomes the guest at the door. Goodbye ends a visit. No thank you answers an offer. A tag question checks a fact, and nothing has been said yet.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: To say again that something is correct. — Confirm means you check a fact and say it is correct. Saying no is refuse. Bringing food to a table is serve. Making a mistake is being wrong.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Pull the door. — The notice says PULL and Don't push, so pull it. Pressing and twisting are different moves. The notice does not ask for either of them.
